title: The four pillars of OOP
scopeHtml: Scope: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism, each tied to a real design decision, with JVM dispatch and vtable depth.

notes.title: The four pillars at a glance
notes.html:
Encapsulation hides data behind rules, abstraction hides complexity behind a simple contract, inheritance reuses a parent's code, polymorphism lets one call do different things depending on the real object. Interviewers do not want the definitions; they want to hear what design decision each pillar buys you and what it costs.

Pillar Real decision Cost if misused
Encapsulation Keep invariants in one class Getter/setter bags give false safety
Abstraction Callers depend on an interface Leaky or premature abstractions
Inheritance Share state/code in a true "is-a" Fragile base class, tight coupling
Polymorphism Replace if/else with dispatch Hard-to-trace call paths

Worked example. A payments module with 4 methods (card, UPI, wallet, netbanking) and 12 if (type == ...) branches in 5 places has 60 places to forget when you add method 5. Pillars 2 and 4 collapse that to 1 new class.

Industry examples. Android View hierarchy (inheritance + polymorphic onDraw), JDBC (abstraction), Java String (encapsulation: immutable, internals can change from char[] to byte[], which happened in Java 9 with compact strings, without breaking callers).

Everyday analogy. A car: the dashboard is the abstraction, the sealed engine bay is encapsulation, "all cars have wheels and an engine" is inheritance, and pressing the accelerator works the same on petrol or electric (polymorphism).

Common interview traps.

  • Reciting definitions with no example from a system you built.
  • Presenting inheritance as the main tool; modern advice is composition first (see the design principles note).

notes.title: Encapsulation: guard the invariant
notes.html:
Encapsulation means an object owns its data and is the only one allowed to change it, so its rules can never be broken from outside. An invariant is a rule that must always be true, such as "balance never below zero" or "end date is after start date".

Mechanism: private fields plus methods that validate. In Java, access is enforced by the compiler and the JVM at link time; reflection can still break in (setAccessible), and since Java 9 modules (JPMS) and since 16/17 strong encapsulation of JDK internals make that harder.

Before (anyone can break the rule):

class Account { public long balance; }
acc.balance -= 5000;          // overdraft, no audit, no thread safety

After (rule enforced in one place, thread-safe):

final class Account {
    private long balance;                          // cents
    synchronized void withdraw(long cents) {
        if (cents <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount");
        if (cents > balance) throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient funds");
        balance -= cents;
    }
    synchronized long balance() { return balance; }
}
class Account {
    var balance = 0L; private set
    @Synchronized fun withdraw(cents: Long) {
        require(cents > 0); check(cents <= balance) { "insufficient funds" }
        balance -= cents
    }
}

Worked example. Two threads each withdraw 700 from a balance of 1000 with an unsynchronised check-then-act: both pass the check (700 <= 1000), both subtract, balance becomes -400. With the lock, the second sees 300 and fails. Real banks do this in the database (UPDATE ... SET balance = balance - 700 WHERE id = ? AND balance >= 700, check rows updated = 1).

  caller --> [ withdraw() ] --guards--> [ private balance ]
  caller -X-----------------------------> direct access blocked

Industry examples. Java's String, BigDecimal and LocalDate are immutable so they can never be left half-changed. Kotlin private set and Android ViewModel exposing StateFlow (read-only) while keeping MutableStateFlow private is the same pattern.

Everyday analogy. An ATM: you cannot reach into the vault, you can only press buttons that follow the bank's rules.

Decision gravity. Private fields with behaviour methods are reversible and cheap now. A public mutable field or a getter that returns the internal List is a one-way door; callers will mutate it. Return List.copyOf(items) or Collections.unmodifiableList(items).

Common interview traps.

  • A getter returning a mutable collection or Date leaks the internals.
  • Auto-generated getters and setters for every field are not encapsulation.
  • Forgetting that encapsulation also covers concurrency: invariants across two fields need one lock.

notes.title: Abstraction: hide the how
notes.html:
Abstraction means showing only what the caller needs and hiding the rest. Encapsulation is about protecting data; abstraction is about simplifying what you present.

Mechanism: interfaces and abstract classes define a vocabulary (send(message)), and implementations hide transport, retries, auth and format. Good abstractions are stable while implementations change.

Before (caller knows SMTP, SMS and push details):

void notifyUser(User u, String text) {
    if (u.prefersEmail) { Properties p = new Properties(); /* 20 lines of SMTP */ }
    else if (u.prefersSms) { /* HTTP to the SMS vendor */ }
}

After:

interface Notifier { void send(String userId, String text); }

class EmailNotifier implements Notifier { public void send(String u, String t) { /* SMTP hidden */ } }
class SmsNotifier   implements Notifier { public void send(String u, String t) { /* vendor HTTP hidden */ } }

class OrderService {
    private final Notifier notifier;
    OrderService(Notifier n) { this.notifier = n; }
    void shipped(String userId) { notifier.send(userId, "Your order shipped"); }
}
fun interface Notifier { fun send(userId: String, text: String) }
class OrderService(private val notifier: Notifier) { fun shipped(userId: String) = notifier.send(userId, "Your order shipped") }

Worked example. Swapping the SMS vendor (vendor A at Rs 0.18/SMS to vendor B at Rs 0.12/SMS) changes one class. At 5M SMS a month that is Rs 300,000 saved, and OrderService is untouched.

Industry examples. JDBC and Android Room hide the database; Retrofit hides HTTP; Kafka producer API hides partitioning and batching. Netflix's Hystrix/Resilience4j wrap calls behind a stable surface.

Everyday analogy. Driving: steering wheel and pedals, not fuel injection timing.

Decision gravity. Abstract at a point of real change (vendors, storage, platforms), not everywhere. A wrong abstraction is worse than duplication: callers shape themselves around it and it becomes a one-way door once public. The "rule of three": wait for the third use before extracting.

Common interview traps.

  • Leaky abstraction: an InMemoryStore interface that exposes flushToDisk().
  • Abstract class vs interface: abstract class carries state and partial code; interface is a contract, and a class can have many.
  • Confusing abstraction (design idea) with the abstract keyword (one tool).

notes.title: Inheritance: reuse with a catch
notes.html:
Inheritance lets a child class get the parent's fields and methods and override some. It models "is-a": a SavingsAccount is an Account.

Mechanism: a child object in memory holds the parent's fields first, then its own, so a child reference can be treated as the parent type (upcast). super(...) runs the parent constructor first. Java has single class inheritance only, to avoid the diamond problem on state; default methods bring limited multiple inheritance of behaviour.

Before (copy-paste):

class CurrentAccount { long bal; void deposit(long c){ bal += c; } void withdraw(long c){ /* 10 lines */ } }
class SavingsAccount { long bal; void deposit(long c){ bal += c; } void withdraw(long c){ /* same 10 lines */ } }

After (genuine is-a, shared code once):

abstract class Account {
    protected long balance;
    void deposit(long c) { balance += c; }
    void withdraw(long c) { if (c > limit()) throw new IllegalStateException(); balance -= c; }
    protected abstract long limit();
}
class Savings extends Account { protected long limit() { return balance; } }
class Current extends Account { protected long limit() { return balance + 50_000; } } // overdraft
abstract class Account(protected var balance: Long = 0) {
    fun deposit(c: Long) { balance += c }
    fun withdraw(c: Long) { check(c <= limit()); balance -= c }
    protected abstract fun limit(): Long
}
class Savings : Account() { override fun limit() = balance }
class Current : Account() { override fun limit() = balance + 50_000 }
        +-----------------+
        |  Account        |
        |  #balance       |
        |  +deposit()     |
        |  +withdraw()    |
        |  #limit()  {abs}|
        +--------^--------+
          +------+------+
   +------+-----+  +----+-------+
   |  Savings   |  |  Current   |
   +------------+  +------------+

Worked example (the catch). Classic Liskov violation: Square extends Rectangle with setWidth also setting height. Code that does r.setWidth(5); r.setHeight(4); area == 20 fails for a Square (gives 16). Inheritance promises a child can stand in for the parent everywhere; if it cannot, it is wrong.

Industry examples. Android AppCompatActivity extends FragmentActivity ... is a deep chain that makes behaviour hard to follow; Google moved towards composition (Jetpack ViewModel, Lifecycle observers). Java's Stack extends Vector is a famous mistake: it exposes insertElementAt, breaking stack discipline. Effective Java: "Design and document for inheritance or else prohibit it" (hence final classes).

Everyday analogy. A family recipe: the child recipe starts as the parent's and tweaks one ingredient; but if you change the parent recipe, every child dish changes too.

Decision gravity. Inheritance is the tightest coupling Java offers; changing a parent can silently break every child (fragile base class). Choose it only for a stable, true is-a with substitutability; prefer composition otherwise. Moving from inheritance to composition later means rewriting every subclass: a one-way door in practice.

Common interview traps.

  • Inheriting just to reuse code when the relationship is "has-a" or "uses-a".
  • Overriding a method that the parent calls inside its own code (self-use) without knowing it.
  • protected fields: they are part of the public API to every subclass, ever.

notes.title: Polymorphism: one call, many behaviours
notes.html:
Polymorphism means the same method call runs different code depending on the real type of the object. shape.area() works for circles and squares without the caller checking which.

Two kinds. Compile-time (overloading): the compiler picks the method from the declared argument types. Runtime (overriding): the JVM picks from the actual object type when the code runs. Interviews usually mean the second.

Before (type-checking by hand):

double area(Object s) {
    if (s instanceof Circle c) return Math.PI * c.r * c.r;
    if (s instanceof Rect r) return r.w * r.h;
    throw new IllegalArgumentException();       // new shape = edit this method
}

After:

sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Rect { double area(); }
record Circle(double r) implements Shape { public double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; } }
record Rect(double w, double h) implements Shape { public double area() { return w * h; } }

double total = shapes.stream().mapToDouble(Shape::area).sum();
sealed interface Shape { fun area(): Double }
data class Circle(val r: Double) : Shape { override fun area() = Math.PI * r * r }
data class Rect(val w: Double, val h: Double) : Shape { override fun area() = w * h }

Worked example. Circle(2) gives about 12.57, Rect(3,4) gives 12. A list of 1,000 mixed shapes is summed in one loop with zero instanceof. Adding Triangle is one new record; the compiler flags exhaustive switch sites for sealed types.

Industry examples. Spring injects different PaymentGateway beans per profile; java.util.List lets you swap ArrayList for LinkedList; Android's RecyclerView.Adapter and Compose's @Composable slots rely on it.

Everyday analogy. Saying "dance" to a crowd: ballet dancers, breakdancers and your uncle each do it their own way.

Decision gravity. Polymorphism is open for new types but closed for new operations (adding perimeter() touches all classes); switch over a sealed type is the reverse. This is the expression problem. Pick polymorphism when types grow, pattern-matching switch when operations grow.

Common interview traps.

  • Overloading is resolved at compile time on the declared type: print(Object o) vs print(String s) with Object x = "hi"; print(x) calls the Object version.
  • Fields and static methods are not polymorphic (they are hidden, not overridden).
  • Overriding with a weaker access modifier or a broader checked exception is illegal.

notes.title: JVM dispatch and the vtable
notes.html:
Under the hood, a virtual call is a lookup in a per-class table of method addresses. Knowing this lets you explain why polymorphism is cheap and when it is not.

Mechanism. Each class has a vtable (virtual method table) in its metadata (HotSpot: Klass). Every instance has an object header with a pointer to its class (the "klass word", 4 bytes with compressed class pointers). A child's vtable starts as a copy of the parent's, and overridden slots are replaced with the child's method; new methods are appended. A call shape.area() compiles to invokevirtual Shape.area; at runtime the VM loads the object's class, reads the vtable slot (a fixed index known at link time), and jumps. Interface calls (invokeinterface) cannot use one fixed index because a class implements many interfaces, so they use an itable search or cached lookup, which is a bit slower when cold.

 Circle object                 Circle.class vtable
 +-----------+                 slot0 toString -> Object.toString
 | header    |--klass-------->  slot1 equals   -> Object.equals
 | r = 2.0   |                 slot2 area     -> Circle.area   <== overridden
 +-----------+                 slot3 perimeter-> Circle.perimeter

What the JIT does. The HotSpot C2 compiler profiles each call site. If it has only ever seen one class (monomorphic) it inlines the method behind a cheap class-check guard, so the call costs about the same as a plain call or less. With two types (bimorphic) it still inlines both with checks. With three or more (megamorphic) it falls back to a real vtable or itable call, roughly a few nanoseconds extra and, more important, it blocks inlining, which blocks later optimisations. Class Hierarchy Analysis also lets it devirtualise a method when only one loaded class overrides it, and deoptimise if a new class loads later. final methods and classes help the compiler, though the JIT often figures it out anyway.

Worked example. A hot loop doing 100M shape.area() calls on one type: JIT inlines, about 0.3 ns/call, roughly 30 ms in total. The same loop over a random mix of 5 types: megamorphic, about 3 to 5 ns/call, roughly 300 to 500 ms. Treat these as order of magnitude; always measure with JMH. In normal business code (network and DB at 1 to 50 ms) this difference is irrelevant; it matters in tight numeric or serialisation loops.

Overload vs override at bytecode level. The overload is chosen by javac and written into the bytecode as a specific method descriptor; the override is chosen at runtime by the vtable. invokestatic, invokespecial (constructors, super.x(), private methods) and invokevirtual are different instructions; invokedynamic powers lambdas and string concatenation.

Industry examples. The Netty and Kafka code bases avoid megamorphic hot paths (a few concrete handler types per call site). The Truffle/Graal and JMH docs discuss type profile pollution, and Java's own Collections code keeps sort comparators cheap this way.

Everyday analogy. A phone book with fixed page numbers per name: the receptionist looks at who you are (header), flips to the fixed page (slot) and dials the number (method).

Decision gravity. Do not hand-optimise away polymorphism for speed; readability wins and the JIT is good. Only restructure a measured hot path (for example, group items by type before looping). This is reversible and local.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "virtual calls are slow"; mostly false after JIT inlining. The honest answer is monomorphic/bimorphic calls are cheap, megamorphic ones are not.
  • Calling an overridable method from a constructor (dispatch uses the real class, but its fields are not yet initialised).
  • Kotlin classes are final by default; you must write open. Java is open by default. Kotlin's override keyword is mandatory.

notes.title: Tying the pillars to a real design
notes.html:
Take one feature, "send a receipt", and use all four pillars on purpose.

  <<interface>> ReceiptChannel        (abstraction)
        ^                 ^
  EmailReceipt        SmsReceipt      (polymorphism: both used via the interface)
        ^
  HtmlEmailReceipt                    (inheritance: only for a true specialisation)

  Receipt { private lines; total() }  (encapsulation: totals computed inside)
final class Receipt {
    private final List<Long> lineCents;
    Receipt(List<Long> l) { this.lineCents = List.copyOf(l); }       // encapsulated + immutable
    long total() { return lineCents.stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum(); }
}
interface ReceiptChannel { void deliver(String to, Receipt r); }     // abstraction
class EmailReceipt implements ReceiptChannel { public void deliver(String to, Receipt r) { /* SMTP */ } }
class SmsReceipt   implements ReceiptChannel { public void deliver(String to, Receipt r) { /* SMS */ } }

class ReceiptService {
    private final List<ReceiptChannel> channels;                      // polymorphism at work
    ReceiptService(List<ReceiptChannel> c) { channels = c; }
    void send(String to, Receipt r) { channels.forEach(ch -> ch.deliver(to, r)); }
}
class Receipt(lines: List<Long>) { private val lineCents = lines.toList(); fun total() = lineCents.sum() }
interface ReceiptChannel { fun deliver(to: String, r: Receipt) }
class ReceiptService(private val channels: List<ReceiptChannel>) {
    fun send(to: String, r: Receipt) = channels.forEach { it.deliver(to, r) }
}

Worked example. Adding WhatsApp receipts (WhatsApp Business API) is 1 new class implementing ReceiptChannel, 0 edits to ReceiptService, plus a test with a fake channel. Cost: 1 afternoon vs 2 days of finding every if (channel == ...).

Industry examples. Uber and Swiggy notification services use a channel interface with push, SMS, email and WhatsApp implementations selected by user preference and cost.

Everyday analogy. A postal service: one "deliver this" contract, many trucks and couriers, and the letter itself sealed in an envelope.

Common interview traps.

  • Naming all four pillars but being unable to show one concrete decision for each.
  • Using inheritance for HtmlEmailReceipt when a format strategy field would do.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Encapsulation guards invariants in one place (private state, validated methods, no leaked mutable internals, locks for concurrent invariants).
  • Abstraction hides the how behind a stable contract; put it at real points of change, wait for the rule of three.
  • Inheritance is for stable, substitutable is-a only; it is the tightest coupling and a one-way door; prefer composition.
  • Polymorphism replaces type-checking with dispatch: open for new types, closed for new operations (expression problem; sealed + switch is the opposite trade).
  • JVM: invokevirtual uses a vtable slot from the object's klass pointer; invokeinterface uses itable lookup; JIT inlines mono/bimorphic sites and slows at megamorphic ones.
  • Overloading is compile-time, overriding is runtime; fields and statics are not polymorphic; never call overridable methods from constructors.

questions.promptHtml: My class has private fields with a getter and setter for each. Is that encapsulation?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It separates people who recite "private fields" from people who know encapsulation means protecting an invariant.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Not really. Encapsulation means the object owns its data and is the only one that can change it, so its rules cannot be broken from outside. A public setter for every field lets any caller put the object into an invalid state, so it is just public fields with extra typing. I expose behaviour like withdraw(cents) that validates, and keep the state private.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
An invariant is a rule that must always hold: "balance never below zero", "end date after start date". Encapsulation puts the check in one place, inside the class. If setBalance(-500) exists, the rule lives in every caller instead, and one caller will forget. Java enforces private through the compiler and JVM, but reflection (setAccessible) can still break in; JPMS and strong encapsulation of JDK internals (Java 16/17) narrow that.

Two more leaks to know: a getter that returns the internal List or Date lets callers mutate your state, and an invariant that spans two fields needs one lock, otherwise threads break it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
final class Account {
    private long balance;                       // cents
    synchronized void withdraw(long cents) {
        if (cents <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount");
        if (cents > balance) throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient funds");
        balance -= cents;
    }
    synchronized long balance() { return balance; }
}
class Account {
    var balance = 0L; private set
    @Synchronized fun withdraw(cents: Long) {
        require(cents > 0); check(cents <= balance) { "insufficient funds" }
        balance -= cents
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• IDE-generated getters and setters for every field and calling it done.
  • Returning a mutable collection from a getter.
  • Forgetting that cross-field invariants also need atomicity.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you return a list safely? -> List.copyOf(items) for a snapshot or Collections.unmodifiableList for a read-only view (the view still changes if the source does).
  2. Can reflection bypass private? -> Yes via setAccessible, unless JPMS strong encapsulation blocks it; it is not a security boundary.
  3. Why is the setter-bag worse than public fields in practice? -> It gives false confidence: reviewers see "encapsulated" and stop checking, but there is no rule enforced anywhere.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "private fields plus getters". The senior answer names the invariant, shows where it is enforced, and mentions concurrency and leaked collections.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams find "negative balance" or "end before start" rows in production, trace them to a setter used by one import job that skipped validation.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between abstraction and encapsulation, and when do I use an interface versus an abstract class?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates confuse the two pillars; the interface-vs-abstract-class part checks practical design judgement.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Encapsulation protects data: private state behind validated methods. Abstraction simplifies what the caller sees: a stable contract like Notifier.send() that hides SMTP, retries and vendor details. Interface for a contract many unrelated classes can implement; abstract class when subclasses share state or partial code and are truly the same kind of thing.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Abstraction is a design idea; the abstract keyword is only one tool. Good abstractions sit at a point of real change (vendors, storage, platforms) and stay stable while implementations vary. The cost is a premature or leaky abstraction: an InMemoryStore interface exposing flushToDisk() leaks one implementation into every caller, and once public it is hard to remove. Rule of three: extract after the third real use.

 OrderService --> Notifier (contract) --> EmailNotifier | SmsNotifier | PushNotifier
Interface Abstract class
State none (constants only) yes
Inheritance a class can implement many one parent only
Use for capability/contract shared skeleton of a family

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface Notifier { void send(String userId, String text); }
class OrderService {
    private final Notifier notifier;
    OrderService(Notifier n) { this.notifier = n; }
    void shipped(String id) { notifier.send(id, "Your order shipped"); }
}
fun interface Notifier { fun send(userId: String, text: String) }
class OrderService(private val notifier: Notifier) {
    fun shipped(id: String) = notifier.send(id, "Your order shipped")
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Equating abstraction with the abstract keyword.
  • Creating an interface for every class "for testability" with only one implementation and no seam.
  • Abstractions that leak implementation methods.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can an interface have code? -> Yes, default and static methods since Java 8, but no instance state.
  2. When does the abstraction become a one-way door? -> When it is public and many callers depend on it; a wrong shape is then expensive to change.
  3. What is the rule of three? -> Tolerate duplication twice, abstract on the third use, when you can see what actually varies.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists syntax differences. The senior says where to put the abstraction (at a real change point), what it costs when wrong, and the rule of three.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Swapping an SMS vendor (Rs 0.18 to Rs 0.12 per SMS, 5M a month, Rs 300,000 saved) is a one-class change only because callers depend on the contract.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between method overloading and overriding, and are fields polymorphic?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A classic that exposes whether you know compile-time vs runtime resolution.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Overloading means same name with different parameter lists, and javac picks one from the declared argument types at compile time. Overriding means a subclass replaces an inherited method, and the JVM picks from the actual object type at runtime. Fields and static methods are not polymorphic; they are hidden, resolved by the declared type.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The compiler writes the chosen method descriptor into the bytecode for overloads. For overrides, invokevirtual uses the object's class at runtime. So Object x = "hi"; print(x) calls print(Object) even though the object is a String, because the declared type is Object.

Override rules: same signature, return type covariant, access cannot be weaker, cannot throw broader checked exceptions. Kotlin needs override and the parent must be open.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class Printer {
    void print(Object o) { System.out.println("Object"); }
    void print(String s) { System.out.println("String"); }
}
Object x = "hi";
new Printer().print(x);      // prints Object (compile-time type)
class Printer {
    fun print(o: Any) = println("Any")
    fun print(s: String) = println("String")
}
val x: Any = "hi"
Printer().print(x)           // prints Any

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Expecting overload choice from the runtime type.
  • Thinking a field with the same name in a subclass overrides the parent's field.
  • Forgetting @Override, so a typo silently creates a new method.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can you override a static method? -> No, you hide it; the call binds to the declared type.
  2. Can an override narrow the return type? -> Yes (covariant return).
  3. Which bytecode instruction does each use? -> Overload: resolved by javac into the descriptor; override: invokevirtual (or invokeinterface).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "compile-time vs runtime". Senior adds the declared-type trap, field hiding, override rules and @Override as a safety net.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An equals(Foo) overload instead of equals(Object) made List.contains fail silently for months.

questions.promptHtml: Are virtual method calls slow in Java? How does the JVM actually dispatch them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can explain polymorphism's cost from the machine up and avoid cargo-cult "avoid interfaces" advice.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Mostly no. A virtual call reads the class pointer from the object header and jumps through a fixed slot in the class's vtable. The JIT profiles each call site: with one or two seen types it inlines behind a cheap guard, so cost is near zero. Only megamorphic sites (three or more types) fall back to a real table call and block inlining.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Each class has a vtable of method addresses; a child copies the parent's, replaces overridden slots and appends new ones. invokevirtual knows the slot index at link time. invokeinterface cannot use one fixed index since a class implements many interfaces, so it searches an itable or uses a cached lookup (slightly slower cold).

 object header --klass--> Circle vtable:  slot2 area -> Circle.area
 call site: load klass, read slot2, jump

C2 also uses Class Hierarchy Analysis: if only one loaded class overrides a method it devirtualises, and deoptimises if a new class loads. Order of magnitude: monomorphic 0.3 ns/call vs megamorphic 3 to 5 ns/call; always verify with JMH. In code dominated by 1 to 50 ms I/O, this is noise.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Virtual calls are slow" as a blanket statement.
  • Marking everything final for speed without measuring.
  • Calling an overridable method from a constructor (dispatch uses the real class, fields not yet initialised).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is monomorphic/bimorphic/megamorphic? -> 1, 2, 3+ receiver types seen at a call site.
  2. How would you fix a hot megamorphic loop? -> Group items by type before looping, so each loop sees one type.
  3. Why are Kotlin classes final by default? -> Design choice for safe inheritance (Effective Java advice); open makes it overridable.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "virtual means slower". Senior explains vtable, type profiles and inlining, and refuses to optimise without JMH evidence.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A serialisation hot path with 6 handler types per call site lost throughput; grouping by type before the loop recovered it.

questions.contextHtml:
A shopping Cart is reviewed. A report job calls cart.getItems(), sorts the result for display, and later the checkout total shows items in the wrong order and the cart's "last added" item is wrong. A second bug: Cart.getCreatedAt() returns a java.util.Date, and a billing helper does cart.getCreatedAt().setTime(...) to shift a window.

class Cart {
    private final List<Item> items = new ArrayList<>();
    private final Date createdAt = new Date();
    public List<Item> getItems() { return items; }
    public Date getCreatedAt() { return createdAt; }
    public void add(Item i) { items.add(i); }
}
// ReportJob
List<Item> sorted = cart.getItems();
Collections.sort(sorted, byName);
questions.promptHtml: Find the bugs, fix the class, and say what kind of decision this was.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add synchronized" or "make a copy in the report job". It fixes one caller, not the class, and the next caller repeats the bug.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do any callers legitimately mutate via getItems() (grep first)? Does Item itself mutate? Is the Cart shared across threads? Is Java 8+ time API available?
  2. Immediate mitigation: In the report job sort a copy: new ArrayList<>(cart.getItems()). That stops the data corruption today.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Leaked internal list (confirmed by the sort), mutable Date leaked, other callers mutating the list.
  4. How I'd verify: Grep callers of getItems(); add a test that sorts the returned list and asserts the cart order unchanged; temporarily return Collections.unmodifiableList and run the suite to find mutators.
  5. Root cause: The class hands out references to its own state, so encapsulation is broken even though fields are private.
  6. Fix: Return a copy or immutable view, use Instant, expose behaviour.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
final class Cart {
    private final List<Item> items = new ArrayList<>();
    private final Instant createdAt = Instant.now();
    List<Item> items() { return List.copyOf(items); }
    Instant createdAt() { return createdAt; }
    void add(Item i) { items.add(Objects.requireNonNull(i)); }
}
class Cart {
    private val _items = mutableListOf<Item>()
    val items: List<Item> get() = _items.toList()
    val createdAt: Instant = Instant.now()
    fun add(i: Item) { _items += i }
}
  1. Prevention: A lint/review rule: no getter returns a mutable collection or Date; tests that mutate returned collections; static analysis (SpotBugs EI_EXPOSE_REP).
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: List.copyOf costs an allocation per call; on a hot path I would return an unmodifiable view. I would not sprinkle defensive copies in every caller.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• unmodifiableList vs copyOf? -> The view reflects later changes to the source; the copy is a snapshot and truly immutable.
  • Cart has 10,000 items and items() is called per request? -> Return an unmodifiable view or stream; measure first.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A pricing bug appeared only after the nightly report ran in the same JVM; a cached catalogue list was sorted in place by a "harmless" getter caller.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: patches the caller only.
  • Hire: copies or views in the getter, replaces Date.
  • Strong hire: also names the rule as a one-way door, adds a test and static-analysis guard.

questions.contextHtml:
A payments module supports card, UPI, wallet and netbanking. The same switch (type) appears in pay(), refund(), fee(), label() and receipt(): 5 places. Product now wants a fifth method, "BNPL", by next Friday. Last quarter someone added wallet and forgot refund(); 14 refunds were silently skipped.

double fee(String type, long cents) {
    switch (type) {
        case "CARD": return cents * 0.02;
        case "UPI": return 0;
        case "WALLET": return cents * 0.005;
        default: throw new IllegalArgumentException(type);
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Which classes change for BNPL today, and how would you restructure so the next method does not repeat this?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Add another case in all five places and a unit test. Works, but keeps the "forget one place" risk.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are operations (pay, refund, fee) going to grow too, or only methods? Is type persisted as a string in the DB? Do we need runtime selection by config? Is there a deadline pressure that forbids a refactor first?
  2. Immediate mitigation: If Friday is tight, add BNPL to all five switches plus a test that iterates every enum value through every operation, then refactor next sprint.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The root issue is type-checking by hand; each new type touches N places; missing ones fail at runtime.
  4. How I'd verify: grep -rn "case \"WALLET\"" to list all sites; a test enumerating all methods against all operations.
  5. Root cause: Behaviour is separated from the type it belongs to.
  6. Fix: One interface, one class per method; the call site no longer checks types.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface PaymentMethod {
    String label();
    long fee(long cents);
    void pay(long cents);
    void refund(long cents);
}
final class Upi implements PaymentMethod { /* fee 0 ... */ public String label(){return "UPI";} public long fee(long c){return 0;} public void pay(long c){} public void refund(long c){} }
// BNPL = one new class; registry maps "BNPL" -> instance
interface PaymentMethod { val label: String; fun fee(cents: Long): Long; fun pay(cents: Long); fun refund(cents: Long) }
object Upi : PaymentMethod { override val label = "UPI"; override fun fee(cents: Long) = 0L; override fun pay(cents: Long) {}; override fun refund(cents: Long) {} }
  1. Prevention: Interface forces every method to implement every operation (compiler catches the missing refund); contract test run against all implementations.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Polymorphism is closed for new operations: adding chargeback() touches all classes. If operations grow faster than types, a sealed interface with a pattern-matching switch is the better shape. I would not build a plugin loader for a method list that changes twice a year.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Operations will grow quickly -> sealed type plus exhaustive switch (expression problem).
  • DB stores "CARD" strings -> keep a factory or enum that maps string to implementation at the edge.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A refund path missing one method type cost a team a week of manual reconciliation; the interface refactor took a day.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds cases everywhere.
  • Hire: interface and one class per method.
  • Strong hire: also names the expression-problem trade-off and the exhaustive contract test.

questions.contextHtml:
A wallet service, 800 withdrawals/s at peak, shows 37 accounts with negative balances after a promo. Logs for one account:

12:00:01.104 [t-17] withdraw acct=A91 amt=700 balance_read=1000
12:00:01.104 [t-23] withdraw acct=A91 amt=700 balance_read=1000
12:00:01.105 [t-17] balance_set=300
12:00:01.105 [t-23] balance_set=300   <- lost update? final read says -400 in ledger

The code is if (acct.getBalance() >= amt) acct.setBalance(acct.getBalance() - amt); in a service class. A red herring: the DB shows no deadlocks and CPU is 30%.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, how do you stop it now, and how do you fix it properly?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add synchronized on the service method." It serialises every account on one lock, does nothing across multiple app instances, and keeps the rule outside the object.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: One app instance or many? Is the balance authoritative in memory or in the DB? Are there other writers (batch, admin tool)? What is the isolation level?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause the promo or cap per-account concurrency; flag negative accounts for review.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Check-then-act race on read-modify-write; second instance with its own cache; non-atomic two-step setBalance.
  4. How I'd verify: Reproduce with a test of 2 threads x 1000 withdrawals; check SELECT acct, balance FROM wallet WHERE balance < 0; see if app instances > 1.
  5. Root cause: Invariant (balance >= 0) is enforced by callers instead of the object/DB, and the check and update are not atomic.
  6. Fix: Short term: one atomic statement. Long term: the entity owns withdraw and the DB enforces it.
UPDATE wallet SET balance = balance - 700 WHERE id = 'A91' AND balance >= 700;
-- rows updated = 1 means success, 0 means insufficient funds
-- plus: ALTER TABLE wallet ADD CONSTRAINT nonneg CHECK (balance >= 0);
  1. Prevention: Concurrency test in CI; DB CHECK constraint; alert on balance < 0; idempotency key per withdrawal.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A JVM synchronized is correct for one instance only. I would not use a global lock. A per-row DB lock or conditional UPDATE scales across instances.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Multiple instances? -> in-process locks are useless; push atomicity to the DB.
  • Hot account with 500 updates/s? -> row contention; queue or batch per account.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "balance never negative" rule lived in 12 callers; one cron job skipped it and quietly overdrew accounts for weeks.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the DB.
  • Hire: spots check-then-act and fixes atomically.
  • Strong hire: moves the invariant into the object and the DB constraint, handles multi-instance.

questions.contextHtml:
A new AuditedReport subclass crashes with an NPE during construction in production, but only for that subclass. Stack trace:

Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException
  at AuditedReport.render(AuditedReport.java:9)
  at BaseReport.<init>(BaseReport.java:6)
  at AuditedReport.<init>(AuditedReport.java:5)
class BaseReport {
    BaseReport() { render(); }               // template call in constructor
    protected void render() { }
}
class AuditedReport extends BaseReport {
    private final List<String> lines = new ArrayList<>();
    AuditedReport() { super(); }
    @Override protected void render() { lines.add("start"); }   // NPE
}
questions.promptHtml: Why does it crash, and what would you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "lines is null because Spring did not inject it" or wrapping in try/catch. Misses the initialisation order.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is BaseReport third party? How many subclasses override render()? Is it ever called outside construction?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move the render() call out of the constructor into an explicit init()/factory step.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Dispatch from super constructor hitting uninitialised subclass field (most likely); DI issue (no, field is plain).
  4. How I'd verify: Read the trace: BaseReport.<init> calls render, which the VM dispatches to AuditedReport.render before the subclass field initialiser has run.
  5. Root cause: Order is: super constructor first, then subclass field initialisers. A virtual call uses the real class, so the override runs on a half-built object.
  6. Fix:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
abstract class BaseReport {
    final void generate() { render(); }      // explicit, after construction
    protected abstract void render();
}
// caller: new AuditedReport().generate();
abstract class BaseReport {
    fun generate() = render()
    protected abstract fun render()
}
  1. Prevention: Static-analysis rule (Sonar S1699: constructors should not call overridable methods); final or private for anything a constructor calls; Kotlin warns "leaking this".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not initialise lines lazily with a null check just to hide it; that preserves the fragile base-class design.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not make render final? -> Then subclasses cannot customise; the whole point of the template.
  • What if lines were a primitive int? -> It reads the default 0, a silent wrong value, worse than an NPE.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A framework base class called an overridable setup() in its constructor; a subclass added a field and only crashed under a particular DI container.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds try/catch.
  • Hire: explains init order, defers the call.
  • Strong hire: names the fragile-base-class problem and a lint rule.

questions.contextHtml:
In review, a teammate wants to count how many elements were ever added to a set, by extending HashSet:

class CountingSet<E> extends HashSet<E> {
    private int added = 0;
    @Override public boolean add(E e) { added++; return super.add(e); }
    @Override public boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) { added += c.size(); return super.addAll(c); }
    int added() { return added; }
}
CountingSet<String> s = new CountingSet<>();
s.addAll(List.of("a", "b", "c"));
System.out.println(s.added());    // prints 6, expected 3

A second team proposes class Stack2 extends ArrayList for a stack. Both are "just reuse".
questions.promptHtml: Why 6, and what is your review comment?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Remove the line in addAll." That works until the JDK changes addAll's self-use; it relies on an undocumented implementation detail.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must it still be a Set for callers? Is the count needed per instance or global? Any chance the JDK version changes?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; block the merge and explain.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: HashSet.addAll (via AbstractCollection) calls add() for each element, so each element is counted twice (3 + 3 = 6).
  4. How I'd verify: Run it; step into addAll and see it call the overridden add.
  5. Root cause: Self-use of an overridable method: the subclass depends on how the parent calls its own methods. That is fragile base class.
  6. Fix: Compose and delegate.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class CountingSet<E> implements Set<E> {
    private final Set<E> inner = new HashSet<>();
    private int added;
    public boolean add(E e) { added++; return inner.add(e); }
    public boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) { added += c.size(); return inner.addAll(c); }
    // other Set methods delegate to inner (IDE can generate; or extend ForwardingSet from Guava)
    int added() { return added; }
}
class CountingSet<E>(private val inner: MutableSet<E> = HashSet()) : MutableSet<E> by inner {
    var added = 0; private set
    override fun add(element: E): Boolean { added++; return inner.add(element) }
    override fun addAll(elements: Collection<E>): Boolean { added += elements.size; return inner.addAll(elements) }
}
  1. Prevention: Review rule: extend only classes designed and documented for inheritance; prefer final; Kotlin's default-final helps.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Delegation costs forwarding boilerplate (Kotlin by, Guava ForwardingSet, Lombok @Delegate). Stack extends Vector and Stack2 extends ArrayList expose add(index, e) and break stack discipline; I would reject both.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can inheritance ever be right? -> Stable true is-a with documented hooks, like AbstractList.
  • Is composition reversible? -> Yes; inheritance to composition later means rewriting every subclass and every caller using the supertype.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A library upgrade changed an internal call and a subclass double-fired events; the team had no way to see the dependency in the diff.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: deletes the addAll override.
  • Hire: explains self-use and delegates.
  • Strong hire: also cites inherited API leakage (Stack) and a design-for-inheritance rule.

questions.contextHtml:
A pricing engine evaluates 100M Rule.apply(Order) calls per batch over 7 rule classes, in a random mixed list. Batch takes 410 ms of pure compute; a JMH run on a single-type list gives 35 ms. A colleague proposes replacing the Rule interface with a giant switch on an int tag "because virtual calls are slow". The whole job then writes to Postgres for 40 s.

JMH: mixed(7 types)  4.1 ns/op
JMH: single type     0.35 ns/op
Batch total wall time: 41 s (compute 0.41 s, DB 40.2 s)
questions.promptHtml: Do you accept the proposal? What do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Either "virtual calls are slow, switch it" or "never think about it". Both skip the measurement and the 40 s DB time.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is batch time the SLO? Is the DB phase fixed? Will rule count grow? Does anything else call apply on a hot path?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; this is not an incident.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The mixed list makes the call site megamorphic (7 > 2 types), blocking inlining; the compute is 1% of wall time anyway.
  4. How I'd verify: JMH numbers above; a profiler flame graph (async-profiler); -XX:+PrintInlining to see "megamorphic" call sites.
  5. Root cause: Type-profile pollution at one call site, real but cheap in absolute terms.
  6. Fix: Reject the switch. If compute ever matters, sort or group orders by rule type so each loop sees one type, a local change hidden behind the method.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
Map<Class<?>, List<Rule>> byType = rules.stream().collect(groupingBy(Object::getClass));
for (List<Rule> group : byType.values())
    for (Rule r : group) r.apply(order);      // each loop call site now sees one type
rules.groupBy { it::class }.values.forEach { group -> group.forEach { it.apply(order) } }
  1. Prevention: JMH benchmark in CI for true hot paths only; profile before optimising.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The switch gives up open/closed and adds a tag to maintain for saving 0.4 s of 41 s. The 40 s DB time (batching, COPY) is where the gain is.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Rules grow to 50? -> Still fine; grouping keeps loops monomorphic.
  • Would final help? -> Marginally; the JIT often infers it; the issue is the receiver mix.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team spent a week de-virtualising an inner loop and saved 20 ms of a 3 s request; the fix that mattered was an N+1 query.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts the switch on folklore.
  • Hire: asks to measure and spots the DB time.
  • Strong hire: explains mono/mega profiles and the grouping trick with numbers.

questions.contextHtml: A geometry library has 12 Shape types, each with area(). Over the next two quarters product expects: 6 new operations (perimeter, boundingBox, toSvg, toJson, collides, simplify) and probably 2 new shapes. A dev says "polymorphism, put every operation as a method on each shape". Another says "make Shape a sealed interface and use pattern-matching switch in separate classes". A third module is a public SDK used by external teams.
questions.promptHtml: Which one do you pick, and how reversible is it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Polymorphism is always the OOP way." It ignores that 6 new operations x 12 classes = 72 edits and pollutes shapes with SVG and JSON concerns.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which axis grows faster, types or operations? Is Shape public API with external implementers? Java version (pattern-matching switch for sealed needs 21; verify for your target)? Are operations rendering concerns that should not live in the model?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design choice).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Operations grow faster (6 vs 2), so the operation axis is the hot one; plain methods suit stable core ops like area().
  4. How I'd verify: Look at git history: how often do new shapes vs new operations appear?
  5. Root cause of the tension: The expression problem: OO makes new types easy and new operations hard; sealed + switch is the reverse.
  6. Decision: Keep area()/perimeter() as methods (core, stable). Put rendering/serialisation in separate operation classes with an exhaustive switch; the compiler flags every site when a new shape is added.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Rect { double area(); }
record Circle(double r) implements Shape { public double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; } }
record Rect(double w, double h) implements Shape { public double area() { return w * h; } }

class SvgRenderer {
    String toSvg(Shape s) {
        return switch (s) {
            case Circle c -> "<circle r='" + c.r() + "'/>";
            case Rect r   -> "<rect w='" + r.w() + "' h='" + r.h() + "'/>";
        };
    }
}
sealed interface Shape { fun area(): Double }
data class Circle(val r: Double) : Shape { override fun area() = Math.PI * r * r }
data class Rect(val w: Double, val h: Double) : Shape { override fun area() = w * h }

fun toSvg(s: Shape): String = when (s) {
    is Circle -> "<circle r='${s.r}'/>"
    is Rect -> "<rect w='${s.w}' h='${s.h}'/>"
}
  1. Prevention: Exhaustive switch without default; ADR documenting which axis we optimise.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: sealed stops external teams adding shapes; if the SDK needs extension, keep an open interface and use a visitor or registry. It is reversible while internal; once public, whichever axis you closed is a one-way door.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• External plugins need new shapes? -> Open interface; operations via visitor or per-type registry.
  • Mixed growth? -> Visitor pattern, or accept the cost on the slower-growing axis.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A model class grew SVG, JSON and PDF methods and every renderer change forced a model release; moving operations out cut release coupling.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "always polymorphism".
  • Hire: names both axes and picks with the growth rate.
  • Strong hire: addresses SDK openness, exhaustive switch and reversibility.

questions.subtopic: All four pillars on one feature
questions.contextHtml: The PM says: "Send a receipt after payment. Email for now, probably SMS and WhatsApp soon, some customers want HTML, some plain text." A dev proposes class HtmlEmailReceipt extends EmailReceipt and class PlainEmailReceipt extends EmailReceipt, and then HtmlSmsReceipt. The receipt totals are computed in ReceiptService with a getter-based Receipt bag.
questions.promptHtml: Ask what you need, then sketch the model using the four pillars, and say where you would NOT use inheritance.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Builds the inheritance matrix (channel x format) and starts coding. Combinatorial subclasses and no invariant owner.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the channel chosen by user preference or cost? Can one payment trigger several channels? Are failures retried (idempotency)? Is "HTML" a body format or a different template per channel? Are totals ever recalculated (tax, discount)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; ship email only, behind the interface, so SMS is additive.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Channel and format vary independently, so inheritance would multiply classes (2 formats x 3 channels = 6); a strategy per axis gives 2 + 3.
  4. How I'd verify: Check the requirement list for a third independent axis; draw the matrix.
  5. Root cause of the wrong design: Using is-a for "varies by".
  6. Design: Encapsulation: immutable Receipt owns lines and total. Abstraction: ReceiptChannel contract. Polymorphism: service loops channels. Inheritance only if a real specialisation exists; formats become a ReceiptFormatter field.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
final class Receipt {
    private final List<Long> lineCents;
    Receipt(List<Long> l) { this.lineCents = List.copyOf(l); }
    long total() { return lineCents.stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum(); }
}
interface ReceiptFormatter { String format(Receipt r); }            // plain | html
interface ReceiptChannel { void deliver(String to, String body); } // email | sms | whatsapp
class ReceiptService {
    private final Map<ReceiptChannel, ReceiptFormatter> routes;
    ReceiptService(Map<ReceiptChannel, ReceiptFormatter> r) { routes = r; }
    void send(String to, Receipt r) { routes.forEach((ch, f) -> ch.deliver(to, f.format(r))); }
}
class Receipt(lines: List<Long>) { private val lineCents = lines.toList(); fun total() = lineCents.sum() }
fun interface ReceiptFormatter { fun format(r: Receipt): String }
fun interface ReceiptChannel { fun deliver(to: String, body: String) }
class ReceiptService(private val routes: Map<ReceiptChannel, ReceiptFormatter>) {
    fun send(to: String, r: Receipt) = routes.forEach { (ch, f) -> ch.deliver(to, f.format(r)) }
}
  1. Prevention: A fake channel in tests; idempotency key per receipt so retries do not double-send.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not build a plugin registry for three channels (YAGNI). Adding WhatsApp is one class and zero edits to ReceiptService.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Channel fails mid-way? -> Per-channel retry with idempotency; do not fail the payment.
  • HTML needs channel-specific tweaks? -> Then template per (channel, format); still composition.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A matrix of subclasses reached 11 classes for 4 channels and 3 formats before someone replaced it with two small strategies.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: subclass matrix.
  • Hire: interface per axis, immutable receipt.
  • Strong hire: asks the right questions first, handles retries and says what is deliberately not built.
